{{Short description|Software system}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=February 2025}}

{{Government by algorithm}}
'''Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions''' ('''COMPAS''')<ref>{{cite web | title=DOC COMPAS | url=https://doc.wi.gov/Pages/AboutDOC/COMPAS.aspx | access-date=2023-04-04}}</ref> is a [[Legal case management|case management]] and [[Decision support software|decision support]] software developed and owned by Northpointe (now Equivant), used by [[U.S. court]]s to assess the likelihood of a [[defendant]] becoming a [[recidivist]].<ref>{{cite news |title=A computer program used for bail and sentencing decisions was labeled biased against blacks. It's actually not that clear. |author=Sam Corbett-Davies, Emma Pierson, Avi Feller and Sharad Goel |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/monkey-cage/wp/2016/10/17/can-an-algorithm-be-racist-our-analysis-is-more-cautious-than-propublicas/ |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=October 17, 2016 |access-date=January 1, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |author=Aaron M. Bornstein |title=Are Algorithms Building the New Infrastructure of Racism? |magazine=[[Nautilus (science magazine)|Nautilus]] |date=December 21, 2017 |url=http://nautil.us/issue/55/trust/are-algorithms-building-the-new-infrastructure-of-racism |access-date=January 2, 2018 |issue=55}}</ref>

COMPAS has been used by the U.S. states of New York, Wisconsin, California, Florida's [[Broward County]], and other jurisdictions.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Kirkpatrick|first=Keith|date=2017-01-23|title=It's not the algorithm, it's the data|journal=Communications of the ACM|language=en|volume=60|issue=2|pages=21–23|doi=10.1145/3022181|s2cid=33993859}}</ref>

== Background ==

COMPAS was created in 1998 by Northpointe, Inc., which merged with other justice technology firms to become '''equivant''' in January 2017.<ref>{{cite web | title=The History of equivant | date=August 28, 2024 | url=https://equivant-court.com/the-history-of-equivant-a-story-of-growth-and-a-commitment-to-simplify-justice/ | publisher=equivant | access-date=2026-03-09}}</ref> It is categorized as a "fourth-generation" risk assessment instrument because it evaluates both static data (such as prior criminal record) and dynamic "criminogenic" needs (such as current social environment and employment status).<ref>{{cite web | title=Risk Assessment Instruments Validated and Implemented in Correctional Settings | url=https://www.ojp.gov/pdffiles1/nij/grants/244620.pdf | publisher=National Institute of Justice | date=2013 | access-date=2026-03-09}}</ref>

While originally designed for correctional rehabilitation planning, its use expanded to judicial sentencing. In 2012, the Wisconsin Department of Corrections adopted COMPAS statewide, a move that later led to the landmark legal challenge in ''[[Loomis v. Wisconsin]]''.<ref>{{cite web | title=The Loomis Case: The Use of Proprietary Algorithms at Sentencing | url=https://www.wisbar.org/NewsPublications/InsideTrack/pages/article.aspx?Volume=9&Issue=14&ArticleID=25730 | publisher=State Bar of Wisconsin | date=2016-06-15 | access-date=2026-03-09}}</ref>

== Risk assessment ==
The COMPAS software uses an algorithm to assess potential recidivism risk. Northpointe created risk scales for general and violent recidivism, and for pretrial misconduct. According to the COMPAS Practitioner's Guide, the scales were designed using behavioral and psychological constructs "of very high relevance to recidivism and criminal careers."{{sfn|Northpointe|2015|p=27}}

; Pretrial release risk scale : Pretrial risk is a measure of the potential for an individual to fail to appear and/or to commit new felonies while on release. According to the research that informed the creation of the scale, "current charges, pending charges, prior arrest history, previous pretrial failure, residential stability, employment status, community ties, and substance abuse" are the most significant indicators affecting pretrial risk scores.{{sfn|Northpointe|2015|p=27}}
;General recidivism scale: The General recidivism scale is designed to predict new offenses upon release, and after the COMPAS assessment is given. The scale uses an individual's criminal history and associates, drug involvement, and indications of juvenile delinquency.{{sfn|Northpointe|2015|p=26}}
;Violent recidivism scale: The violent recidivism score is meant to predict violent offenses following release. The scale uses data or indicators that include a person's "history of violence, history of non-compliance, vocational/educational problems, the person's age-at-intake and the person's age-at-first-arrest."{{sfn|Northpointe|2015|p=28}}

The violent recidivism risk scale is calculated as follows:

<math>s = a(-w) + a_{\text{first}}(-w) + h_{\text{violence}}w + v_{\text{edu}}w + h_{\text{nc}}w</math>

where <math>s</math> is the violent recidivism risk score, <math>w</math> is a weight multiplier, <math>a</math> is current age, <math>a_{\text{first}}</math> is the age at first arrest, <math>h_{\text{violence}}</math> is the history of violence, <math>v_{\text{edu}}</math> is vocational education scale, and <math>h_{\text{nc}}</math> is history of noncompliance. The weight, <math>w</math>, is "determined by the strength of the item's relationship to person offense recidivism that we observed in our study data."{{sfn|Northpointe|2015|p=29}}

== Support and criticism ==
Risk assessment tools such as COMPAS are used because of the desire for objective, evidence-based sentencing procedures as well as increased efficiency in the court system.<ref name="Scaria2024"/> Proponents of using AI and algorithms in the courtroom tend to argue that these solutions will mitigate [[cognitive biases|predictable biases and errors]] in judges' reasoning, such as the [[hungry judge effect]] (the phenomenon that judges are more likely to make lenient decisions after eating a meal).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chatziathanasiou |first1=Konstantin |title=Beware the Lure of Narratives: "Hungry Judges" Should Not Motivate the Use of "Artificial Intelligence" in Law |journal=German Law Journal |date=May 2022 |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=452–464 |doi=10.1017/glj.2022.32 |s2cid=249047713 |language=en |issn=2071-8322|doi-access=free }}</ref> Alternatives to risk assessment tools are possible, but are difficult to implement.<ref name="CHRLR2020"/>

A general critique of the use of proprietary software such as COMPAS is that since the algorithms it uses are [[trade secret]]s, they cannot be examined by the public and affected parties, which has been described as a violation of due process.<ref name="CHRLR2020"/><ref name="The Atlantic" /> Additionally, simple, transparent and more interpretable algorithms have been shown to perform predictions approximately as well as the COMPAS algorithm.<ref name="CHRLR2020"/><ref>{{cite journal |title=Learning Certifiably Optimal Rule Lists for Categorical Data|first1=Elaine|last1=Angelino|first2=Nicholas|last2=Larus-Stone|first3=Daniel|last3=Alabi|first4=Margo|last4=Seltzer|first5=Cynthia|last5=Rudin|date=June 2018|journal=Journal of Machine Learning Research|volume=18|issue=234|pages=1–78|arxiv=1704.01701 |url=https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/v18/17-716.html|access-date=2023-07-20}}</ref> Existing analyses of the algorithms have used the publicly available questionnaires and reverse-engineered approximations based on the publicly available data.<ref name="CHRLR2020"/>

Another general criticism of machine-learning based algorithms is that since they are data-dependent, if the data are biased, the software will likely yield biased results.<ref name="WMD">{{cite book |last=O'Neil |first=Cathy |date=2016 |title=Weapons of Math Destruction |isbn=978-0-553-41881-1 |pages=87|publisher=Crown }}</ref> Similarly, the initial version of the related LSI-R algorithm was primarily trained on Caucasian offenders, which resulted in lower validity for black and Latino offenders.<ref name="CHRLR2020"/> Algorithms may also exhibit other types of bias which are given less attention due to the focus on racial bias.<ref name="Scaria2024"/>

COMPAS risk assessments have been argued to violate [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution|14th Amendment]] [[Equal Protection]] rights on the basis of race, since the algorithms are argued to be racially discriminatory, to result in disparate treatment, and to not be narrowly tailored.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Thomas|first1=C.|last2=Nunez|first2=A.|date=2022|title=Automating Judicial Discretion: How Algorithmic Risk Assessments in Pretrial Adjudications Violate Equal Protection Rights on the Basis of Race|journal=[[Law & Inequality]]|language=en|volume=40|issue=2|pages=371–407|url=https://scholarship.law.umn.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1680&context=lawineq|doi=10.24926/25730037.649|doi-access=free}}</ref> 

== Accuracy ==

Empirical analysis of algorithmic risk assessment tools was inspired by a 2016 [[ProPublica]] investigation of COMPAS and a subsequent study by Dressel and Farid (2018).<ref name="Scaria2024"/> ProPublica found that COMPAS was racially biased against black defendants,<ref name="ProPublica">{{cite journal |last1=Angwin |first1=Julia |last2=Larson |first2=Jeff |date=2016-05-23 |title=Machine Bias |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing |journal=ProPublica |access-date=2019-11-21 }}</ref><ref name="The Atlantic">{{cite news |last=Yong |first=Ed |date=2018-01-17 |title=A Popular Algorithm Is No Better at Predicting Crimes Than Random People |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2018/01/equivant-compas-algorithm/550646/ |access-date=2019-11-21 }}</ref><ref name="New York Times">{{cite news |last=Israni |first=Ellora |date=2017-10-26 |title=When an Algorithm Helps Send You to Prison (Opinion)|work=The New York Times | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/26/opinion/algorithm-compas-sentencing-bias.html |access-date=2019-11-21 }}</ref> and Northpointe responded that the algorithm predicted recidivism accurately regardless of race.<ref name="CHRLR2020"/> Counterintuitively, both statements are true: they refer to two mutually exclusive definitions of [[Fairness (machine learning)|fairness]].<ref name="CHRLR2020">{{cite journal|first=Jacob |last=Humerick| title=Reprogramming Fairness: Affirmative Action in Algorithmic Criminal Sentencing|journal=Columbia Human Rights Law Review Online |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=213–245 |year=2020 |url=https://hrlr.law.columbia.edu/files/2020/04/8-Humerick_FINAL.pdf}}</ref> ProPublica's analysis focused on the rate of classification errors (the chance that a defendant's recidivism is predicted incorrectly), while Northpointe focused on the accuracy of prediction (whether the algorithm treats all defendants equally). If the algorithm is fair on one metric, it will be biased on the other.<ref name="CHRLR2020"/>

The study by Dressel and Farid (2018) found that COMPAS software is somewhat more accurate than individuals with little or no criminal justice expertise, yet less accurate than groups of such individuals.<ref name="Science Advances">{{cite journal |last1=Dressel |first1=Julia |last2=Farid |first2=Hany |date=2018-01-17 |title=The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism |journal=Science Advances |volume=4 |issue=1 |article-number=eaao5580 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aao5580  |pmid=29376122 |pmc=5777393 |bibcode=2018SciA....4.5580D |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="The Atlantic" /> However, a subsequent review found that these results "seem[ed] like a specific occurrence and less reflective of general and real conditions" and that algorithms performed better than humans under conditions closer to the real world.<ref name="Scaria2024"/> For example, a replication study found that the algorithms did better when the chance ([[base rate]]) of rearrest was low, while Dressel and Farid assumed that recidivism and non-recidivism were about equally likely.<ref name="Scaria2024">{{cite journal | last1=Scaria | first1=Arul George | last2=Subramanian | first2=Vidya | last3=George | first3=Nevin K. | last4=Sengupta | first4=Nandana | title=Algorithms and Recidivism: A Multi-disciplinary Systematic Review | journal=Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society | volume=7 | date=16 October 2024 | issn=3065-8365 | doi=10.1609/aies.v7i1.31724 | pages=1292–1305 | url=https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AIES/article/view/31724 | access-date=7 April 2026}}</ref>

Risk assessment tools do not explicitly incorporate race, and doing so would likely violate the US constitution.<ref name="CHRLR2020"/> However, because factors such as education level or employment status are correlated with race, algorithms using these factors produce different results for different racial groups.<ref name="CHRLR2020"/> 

One of the proposed benefits of risk assessment tools is an expected reduction in incarceration rates.<ref name="Scaria2024"/> In 2024, an analysis of the practical impact of <abbr>COMPAS</abbr> in [[Broward County, Florida|Broward County]] found that its use led to a reduced rate of confinement across demographic groups, but that it also exacerbated the differences between racial groups.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Bahl |first1=Utsav |last2=Topaz |first2=Chad |last3=Obermüller |first3=Lea |last4=Goldstein |first4=Sophie |last5=Sneirson |first5=Mira |date=2024-05-22 |title=Algorithms in Judges' Hands: Incarceration and Inequity in Broward County, Florida |url=https://www.uclalawreview.org/algorithms-in-judges-hands-incarceration-and-inequity-in-broward-county-florida/ |access-date=2025-03-10 |website=UCLA Law Review |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Legal rulings ==

In July 2016, the Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled that COMPAS risk scores can be considered by judges during sentencing, but there must be warnings given to the scores to represent the tool's "limitations and cautions."<ref name=":0" />
